questions.q: Why is Meridian's product catalog a document-database problem rather than a relational one?
options: Categories don't share attributes, forcing either mostly-NULL columns or an EAV pattern that degrades query performance as it grows — a document per product avoids both
MongoDB is simply faster than SQL Server for all workloads
Relational databases cannot store product data of any kind
The catalog only has one category, making a document model unnecessary
questions.explain: A tent and a pair of boots have entirely different fields; a document lets each product carry only its own relevant fields without schema migration.

questions.q: Why does 'customers who bought this also bought' get worse over time in a relational model, per this lesson?
options: It requires an expensive multi-hop self-join across orders and order_items, and each additional hop (e.g. 'go one hop further') makes the join more expensive, not less
Relational databases cannot express joins at all
The query gets faster over time as more indexes are added automatically
This type of query has nothing to do with the number of hops involved
questions.explain: Multi-hop self-joins scale poorly, and marketing's natural next request ('one hop further') makes the relational approach progressively worse.

questions.q: What is the real reason Meridian's cart/session problem is a Cosmos DB fit rather than a MongoDB or Neo4j fit?
options: It's a distribution problem, not a modeling problem — simple data that needs low-latency reads/writes from multiple continents at once, which Cosmos DB provides via multi-region distribution and consistency levels
Cart data is too complex to model in any other database
MongoDB and Neo4j cannot store simple key-value-style data
Cosmos DB is chosen purely because it's made by Microsoft
questions.explain: The cart data itself is simple; what SQL Server and even single-region Azure SQL can't do is serve it with low latency from multiple regions at once.

questions.q: What consistency level does this lesson identify as a textbook fit for Meridian's cart/session service?
options: Session consistency — a shopper always sees their own writes immediately, without paying for full global strong consistency
Eventual consistency, since cart accuracy doesn't matter
Strong consistency, since it's the only level Cosmos DB supports
There is no meaningful difference between consistency levels for this use case
questions.explain: Session consistency matches the real requirement: a shopper's own writes are immediately visible, without the cost of full global strong consistency.

questions.q: What common thread does this lesson highlight across all three of Meridian's platform decisions?
options: Each choice came from what the data actually looks like and how it's actually read — the access pattern — not a preference for one database
All three decisions were based on which vendor offered the lowest price
Nobody actually evaluated the specific business problems before choosing a platform
The three decisions were made arbitrarily, with no consistent reasoning
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames this as the same access-pattern-first discipline built since Lesson 1, applied to one continuous business.
